name: Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: an AI catastrophe kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: The Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS, Washington) researches policy on advanced AI and national security (frontier security and AI-enabled cyber attacks, compute policy such as export controls, chip smuggling and location verification, US-China strategy), briefs officials in Washington and runs a three-month AI Policy Fellowship (28 fellows in 2025). This model covers all its work in 2025, when it was still a project of Rethink Priorities ($3.9M of programme spending in its sponsor's audited accounts and Form 990, about $4.2M with its share of the sponsor's central costs); it became a separate charity in 2026. At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from {{low}} to {{high}} on the model's own ranges, so the result is mostly uncertainty: each dollar of its research and policy work is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), the fellows' later work at a typical dollar of such work, credited to the fellowship in full because no other programme is known to have trained the same people (the employers who pay for it are under the mobiliser's share), deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate; the fellowship gives most of the result, no measure it worked on had become law by the end of 2025, and the next dollar counts at 38.5% of the past average. A fifth of the work is aimed at misuse (its cyber work) and its US-China framing adds a race risk; the biggest swings are the chance of an AI catastrophe (the slider), Rethink's typical cut per dollar for misuse work, the mobiliser's share, the years a cut counts and the share of fellows who work on the risk because of the fellowship, and every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

rows.explainer: All of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy's (IAPS) spending in 2025, every programme modelled: research by its Frontier Security, Compute Policy and International Strategy teams, policy engagement in Washington, and the AI Policy Fellowship. IAPS was then a project of Rethink Priorities, which reported it as its own programme line in its Form 990 (line 4b, $3,905,273, grants of $338,292 included) inside its audited consolidated accounts; IAPS became a separate 501(c)(3) (EIN 32-0839313) in 2026 and has filed no return of its own yet (the IRS e-file index, retrieved 14 November 2026, has none). The line is counted here, not in Rethink Priorities' cost, so the spending is counted once. Cost and outputs are the same year (2025).

rows.label: Rethink Priorities' central costs (management, fundraising) carried for IAPS, as a share of its direct spending
rows.explainer: Our judgment. IAPS's line in the Form 990 is programme spending only; the sponsor's finance, HR, legal, compliance and fundraising served it too and are in Rethink Priorities' $3.34M of management and fundraising (accounts p. 4), not split by project. Anchor: about 70% of those central costs serving Rethink Priorities' own departments, our judgment, leaves about $1.0M for $15.65M of sponsored and incubated projects' spending, 6.5% of their direct costs. Range 3% (most of IAPS's operations were its own five-person team) to 11% (50% of central costs for its departments, which leaves $1.67M, 11%, for the projects). The accounts release $5.10M of IAPS's restricted money in 2025 (Note 3) against $3.91M of programme spending; that gap isn't added, because central costs beyond this split would be counted twice in Rethink Priorities' own cost, which keeps the rest, and releases also follow grant terms rather than the year's spending.

rows.label: AI: share of the AI spending on work against misuse (dangerous-capability evaluations, defences against misuse)
rows.explainer: Of IAPS's catastrophe-relevant research and policy work, the share aimed at people using AI to do harm. Its Frontier Security team (11 of 20 researchers on the team page) works on AI-enabled cyber attacks: the 2025 reports on differential access for cyber defence and on the reported autonomous cyber campaign, and part of the data centre security work (theft of model weights by attackers). The rest is aimed at both misuse and loss of control or at neither in particular, so it counts as misalignment work, as the family's rule says: chain-of-thought monitorability, AI agent governance, AI security talent and surge capacity in government, compute policy (export controls, chip smuggling, location verification; 6 researchers) and international strategy (3). Two of the year in review's 8 major items are cyber work (differential access; the autonomous cyber campaign), so 20%, our judgment, 10% (the cyber items as part-time work) to 30% (data centre security and the surge-capacity work counted as misuse too). The result moves almost in proportion with this share, because Rethink Priorities' typical misuse project cuts deaths in survivable catastrophes far more per dollar than its misalignment one.

AI field work: share of the research and policy work that bears on catastrophic risk
rows.explainer: Not all IAPS's work is about catastrophes: part of its compute and international work is about US competitiveness and the contest with China as such (export promotion, chip supply chains, keeping a lead), and some security work is about ordinary national-security harms; that part is valued in unmodelled_benefits_adj, not through the catastrophe chances. Most of it bears on the risk: frontier security (cyber, autonomy, assurance, preparedness for AI crises), governance of frontier compute (location verification, hardware-enabled mechanisms, chip smuggling), chain-of-thought monitorability, agent governance and verification for international agreements. 80%, our judgment, 60% to 95%.

rows.label: AI field work: uptake against a typical project

source.title: IAPS 2025 Year in Review (letter from the executive director, 31 December 2025)
source.quote: We contributed to America's AI Action Plan, with recommendations reflected in provisions on location verification and R&D priorities.

rows.explainer: IAPS's catastrophe-relevant research and policy work against Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project. Above typical in reach: recommendations reflected in the AI Action Plan's provisions on location verification and research priorities, its research used in two bills (location verification in the Chip Security Act, a whistleblower programme at the Bureau of Industry and Security in Stop Stealing our Chips), briefings for congressional and executive staff (the sponsor's Schedule C reports direct lobbying contacts by IAPS staff on AI governance and export controls), over 40 media features, co-authored international reports on verification. Below in how directly it acts: none of it was law or rule by the end of 2025, and policy research cuts the risk only through what governments then do. Net 1, a typical project, our judgment, 0.5 to 1.2 (the family's ceiling).

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted: the fifth of the work left out of the catastrophe chain (catastrophe_relevant_share) informs national-security and competitiveness policy; cyber-defence and data-centre security work also guards against attacks far smaller than a catastrophe; fellows' own research during the fellowship; public understanding through over 40 media features. 10% (2% to 30%) of the modelled value, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): IAPS builds no capabilities, but much of its work is framed as helping the US win the AI contest with China ('protect innovation', faster data-centre security, the Action Plan's acceleration agenda), which can feed a race and speed frontier development; export controls may also slow rivals. -5%, our judgment, down to -15%, because the US-China framing runs through much of the work.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: IAPS publishes analyses of AI-enabled cyber attacks (the autonomous cyber campaign, differential access), which could point attackers to a path; they are policy analyses aimed at defence and give no instructions. -1%, our judgment, down to -5%.
